analysis.one_liner: Bans broadband providers from blocking or throttling lawful internet traffic, while locking in lighter federal rules and preempting state net neutrality laws.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with one Republican cosponsor, was referred to the House Energy and Committee's communications subcommittee and never received a hearing or vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would write into law a basic rule that internet providers cannot block lawful websites or slow down lawful traffic based on what the content is. But it goes further: it declares broadband an 'information service' under light-touch rules, forbids the FCC from ever expanding those open-internet requirements through rulemaking, bars states from passing their own net neutrality laws, and makes broadband eligible for federal universal service subsidies. Supporters cast it as a permanent, middle-ground net neutrality law; critics saw it as trading a modest consumer protection for locking in the industry's preferred, weaker regulatory framework.
analysis.who_benefits: Internet users would gain a permanent federal ban on blocking and throttling of lawful traffic, enforceable through FCC complaint procedures. Broadband providers would gain more: a permanent light-touch classification that limits FCC authority, a shield against stricter state net neutrality laws, and eligibility for federal universal service subsidies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently prohibits broadband providers from blocking lawful content, applications, services, or non-harmful devices, subject to reasonable network management.
It prohibits impairing or degrading lawful internet traffic on the basis of content, application, service, or device — the practice known as throttling.
It requires the FCC to adopt formal complaint procedures within 60 days of enactment to enforce the blocking and throttling bans.
It makes broadband internet access service eligible for funding from federal universal service support mechanisms, opening subsidy money to providers.

analysis.who_pays: The costs fall on broadband providers only lightly, since blocking and throttling are not central to their business. The larger cost falls on the public side of the ledger: the FCC would be barred from expanding open-internet rules by regulation, states would be barred from enacting their own net neutrality laws, and the bill does not explicitly ban paid prioritization ('fast lanes'). Enforcement would run only through individual complaints, a process that favors large providers with legal resources.

drawbacks.text: The bill caps the FCC's authority: the commission may enforce the stated rules but is expressly prohibited from expanding the openness obligations through rulemaking or otherwise, freezing consumer protections at 2019 levels no matter how the internet changes.
It preempts all state and local internet openness laws, overriding stricter state net neutrality statutes.
It declares broadband to be an 'information service,' the light-touch legal classification broadband providers sought, limiting the FCC's broader authority over the industry.

The throttling ban reaches only traffic 'impaired or degraded' on the basis of content — it does not expressly prohibit paid prioritization arrangements, leaving open the possibility of fast lanes for companies willing to pay.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The permanent ban on blocking and throttling is a genuine consumer protection, and the bill's complaint-based enforcement would give it legal force. But the price is steep for anyone who wanted more: the FCC's hands would be tied against future rulemaking, states would be barred from setting tougher rules of their own, and paid fast lanes are not expressly banned. Net neutrality advocates at the time treated bills of this shape as a trade that favors providers — a modest floor in exchange for a permanent ceiling.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 8, 2019, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Communications and Technology subcommittee the next day, and sat there without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Smucker introduced the bill on April 8, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
On April 9, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, where it remained for the rest of the 116th Congress with no further action.
The bill attracted only a single cosponsor in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers came out ahead in the narrow sense that no new federal mandate was imposed on them, and the light-touch regulatory framework they preferred stayed in place. Internet users kept the ability of states to craft their own net neutrality protections, since the bill's preemption of state law never became law.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Smucker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.role: Chair and majority of the committee with jurisdiction over the bill
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill died in committee.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a Republican sponsor and a single Republican cosponsor; with Democrats holding the House majority and the committee gavel, no committee action was ever taken beyond the initial referral.

industries.industry: Broadband internet providers (cable and telecom, e.g. Comcast, Verizon, AT&T)
industries.note: The bill would give them federal universal service subsidies, permanent information-service classification, capped FCC authority, and preemption of state net neutrality laws — while imposing a blocking and throttling ban they could live with. The net effect locks in the industry's preferred light-touch framework, and paid fast lanes are not expressly banned.

industries.industry: Big internet platforms and streaming services
industries.note: They would keep the protection of a ban on blocking and throttling of their traffic, but lose the prospect of stronger rules against paid prioritization under a permanently capped FCC. Their interest in an open internet runs alongside users' interests here.

industries.industry: State governments with net neutrality laws
industries.note: The bill would bar every state and locality from adopting or enforcing any internet openness requirements, taking regulatory power away from states that had moved to set stricter rules than the federal government.
